medical.title: Women bear the brunt of alcohol-related fear, Australian research finds
medical.summary: Women are nearly three-quarters more likely than men to experience fear because of other people's alcohol consumption, University of Queensland research published in the International Journal of Drug Policy has found.

medical.title: When we eat helps set the liver's metabolic rhythms
medical.summary: When we think about metabolism, we usually ask, "What did I eat? How much sugar, fat or protein was in the meal?" But through our research, we have become interested in another question: "When did I eat it?" This matters because metabolism does not work at the same pace throughout the day.

medical.title: Residential context has larger impact on ovarian cancer survival in Black women
medical.summary: Residential context has a stronger association with survival for Black than White women with epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC), according to a study published online Aug. 10 in JAMA Network Open.

medical.title: Targeting two proteins to prevent pulmonary hypertension
medical.summary: UIC researchers have identified two therapeutic targets for pulmonary arterial hypertension, an as-yet-incurable disease that can be caused by a parasite laying eggs in the abdomen. The targets represent an opportunity to diagnose, prevent and treat the life-threatening condition. The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

medical.title: Exercise alters brain activity during cognitive tasks, advanced imaging finds
medical.summary: Researchers at AIST, in collaboration with the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center in the United States, examined changes in brain activity during cognitive tasks before and after acute aerobic exercise in healthy young and older adults. The study is published in the Journal of Magnetic Resonance Imaging.

medical.title: How HIV affects the eyes of aging adults
medical.summary: Older adults with well-controlled HIV may have a higher prevalence of certain eye conditions, particularly dry eye, compared with similar adults without HIV, according to a new study led by a University of Colorado Anschutz Department of Ophthalmology faculty member.

medical.title: Daraxonrasib demonstrates initial antitumor activity in RAS-mutant lung cancer
medical.summary: Daraxonrasib, an oral RAS inhibitor therapy, achieved durable responses in pretreated patients with RAS-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in a phase 1/2 trial led by The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

medical.title: Less-intensive drug combination is more effective in treating acute myeloid leukemia, clinical trial finds
medical.summary: Investigators from the Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute have found that adults with newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) receiving a less-intensive combination of azacitidine and venetoclax had more than twice as much time before treatment failed, the leukemia returned or worsened, or they died, compared with patients receiving intensive chemotherapy. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the findings could change the initial treatment approach for many patients with AML.

medical.title: Autism diagnoses rising fastest among girls and women, study finds
medical.summary: A new Saint Louis University study of nearly a decade of health records finds that the recent rise in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnoses is being driven largely by girls and women, who are being identified at significantly higher rates than in years past, often years later than boys and men.

medical.title: Genetic pathway offers new insight into timing of early brain development
medical.summary: Melbourne researchers have uncovered a critical signaling pathway that controls the timing of brain development, shedding new light on how neurodevelopmental disorders may develop. The research, led by Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI) and published in Nature Communications, has revealed the genetic processes that shape brain development and what can happen when they are disrupted.

medical.title: In Canada, immigration status is associated with length of ICU stay after stroke
medical.summary: Among people who have a stroke in Canada, immigrants were admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) at similar rates to long-term residents or people who were born in Canada, but they were more likely to have longer stays in the ICU, according to a study published Sept. 2, 2026, in Neurology.

medical.title: Mini-tumors reveal new drug combinations for liver cancer
medical.summary: Liver cancer is difficult to treat because tumors vary greatly from patient to patient. Researchers at the University of Basel have captured this diversity by creating a collection of mini-tumors, which they use to systematically search for new treatment options. They tested more than 1,600 compounds using these organoids and used the results to develop promising drug combinations.

medical.title: Novel spatial technology may improve our understanding of cancer biology
medical.summary: Northwestern Medicine scientists have developed a novel high-resolution spatial genomics platform that may enhance future research into how genome organization and genetic alterations contribute to disease development, including cancer, as detailed in a recent study published in Nature Methods.

medical.title: Researchers followed 400,000 kids for 20 years and found a lasting pre-K advantage
medical.summary: A 20-year study of 400,000 students found that children who attended public school pre-K earned better grades and test scores through high school than those in other childcare settings. Better-trained teachers and earlier exposure to structured classrooms may help explain why the advantage lasted so long.

medical.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based meat alternatives. Every one contained fungal toxins
medical.summary: Every one of 212 plant-based meat alternatives and drinks tested in the UK contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, though concentrations remained below recommended EU guideline levels. Researchers say the bigger question is whether regularly eating large amounts of these foods could lead to potentially concerning cumulative exposure over time.

medical.title: The ex-oil executive trying to wean us off fossil fuels
medical.summary: Samantha Cooper once helped power the oil industry. Now she’s fighting to end its hold on our future The post The ex-oil executive trying to wean us off fossil fuels appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: A major Alzheimer’s risk gene may shrink brain cells years before symptoms
medical.summary: Researchers have uncovered a possible reason why the Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 can disrupt the brain long before memory problems begin. In mice, APOE4 increased a protein called Nell2, shrinking neurons and making memory circuits unusually active. That early hyperactivity predicted worse memory later in life. Reducing Nell2 in adult mice reversed the abnormal changes, raising hopes for a new way to intervene before Alzheimer’s progresses.

medical.title: The dental crown of the future could be 3D-printed while you wait
medical.summary: Researchers have found a way to slash the processing time for 3D-printed zirconia crowns from as much as 100 hours to under 30 minutes. The advance could eventually let dentists print strong, customized permanent crowns for patients within a single appointment.

medical.title: A hidden “on switch” in human DNA has finally been decoded
medical.summary: Researchers have used AI to uncover the DNA signature of a key genetic “switch” involved in turning genes on. After analyzing about 500,000 DNA sequences, the model identified the initiator in roughly 60% of human genes. The breakthrough could help predict the effects of harmful mutations and eventually contribute to decoding the broader genetic instructions that control gene activity throughout the body.

medical.title: Experimental compound helps burn fat without muscle loss
medical.summary: A decades-old compound may point to a new way of treating obesity by making the body burn more energy rather than simply reducing appetite. In mice, TOFA increased energy use by as much as 18%, reduced body fat without significant muscle loss, and improved blood sugar, triglycerides, and fatty liver disease. It also produced stronger results when combined with GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound.

medical.title: Cannabis use linked to 37% higher stroke risk in massive study
medical.summary: A massive analysis involving more than 100 million people has found strong links between recreational drug use and stroke, including among younger adults. Cocaine was associated with nearly double the risk of stroke, amphetamines with more than double the risk, and cannabis with a 37% increase.

medical.title: This common vitamin was linked to 13% better cognitive scores
medical.summary: Older adults with mild cognitive impairment and sleep problems who took at least 5,000 IU of vitamin D daily scored more than 13% higher on a cognitive test than those taking none. The preliminary findings suggest vitamin D could be worth studying as a potentially modifiable factor during an early window of cognitive decline.

science.title: Farming experts tout 'conscious' food systems to fix agriculture woes
science.summary: Farmers around the world are struggling with the impact of climate change, financial pressures and depleted soil—and industry experts say bringing consumers closer to the people who produce their food could provide a solution.

science.title: Electron spin unlocks magnetic control of hydrogen surface reactions
science.summary: Chemical reactions at surfaces play a central role in many processes, including catalysis and materials synthesis. It is well known that the outcome of these reactions is influenced by the translational, vibrational and rotational motions of atoms and molecules. Now, a study shows that electron spin, another fundamental property of matter, also influences how chemical reactions at surfaces unfold.

science.title: Heavy water's atmospheric fingerprints boost weather forecasts for up to five days
science.summary: Weather forecasts rely on many different kinds of data, including temperature, humidity and wind. For the first time, researchers, including those at the University of Tokyo, have demonstrated that a long-theorized improvement to weather models—adding data on water isotopes in the atmosphere—does work. They showed that incorporating satellite measurements of water vapor isotopes into weather models improves forecasts of atmospheric conditions for up to five days, including predictions of heavy rainfall in many regions.

science.title: AI boom is testing tech firms' climate pledges
science.summary: Technology companies are stepping up their climate commitments but not fast enough to counter rapidly growing energy needs linked to the artificial intelligence boom, a report said Wednesday.

science.title: In Chile, injured penguins sport copper vests to help them heal
science.summary: Researchers in Chile have designed an unlikely new garment for injured penguins—snug red vests threaded with copper and zinc that they hope will help the aquatic birds heal faster.

science.title: Underwater meadows sustain millions in extreme poverty
science.summary: A study provides the first large-scale empirical evidence that seagrass meadows act as a critical safety net for millions of coastal people living in extreme poverty across the Indo-Pacific.

science.title: The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
science.summary: Star formation across the universe has fallen dramatically over the past 4.5 billion years, but astronomers have uncovered a surprising twist: the supply of neutral hydrogen, a key ingredient for making stars, has barely declined. Using China’s FAST radio telescope and data from roughly 2.5 million galaxies observed by DESI, researchers found that star formation was about 2.5 times higher 4.5 billion years ago, while neutral hydrogen levels were only about 1.4 times higher.

science.title: September brings a dazzling Venus and a glowing Harvest Moon
science.summary: September’s sky features brilliant Venus, the Milky Way’s hazy center, and the seasonal turning point of the equinox. The month ends with a glowing Harvest Moon rising near Saturn and faint Neptune.

environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

mix_items.title: Electron spin unlocks magnetic control of hydrogen surface reactions
mix_items.summary: Chemical reactions at surfaces play a central role in many processes, including catalysis and materials synthesis. It is well known that the outcome of these reactions is influenced by the translational, vibrational and rotational motions of atoms and molecules. Now, a study shows that electron spin, another fundamental property of matter, also influences how chemical reactions at surfaces unfold.

mix_items.title: Heavy water's atmospheric fingerprints boost weather forecasts for up to five days
mix_items.summary: Weather forecasts rely on many different kinds of data, including temperature, humidity and wind. For the first time, researchers, including those at the University of Tokyo, have demonstrated that a long-theorized improvement to weather models—adding data on water isotopes in the atmosphere—does work. They showed that incorporating satellite measurements of water vapor isotopes into weather models improves forecasts of atmospheric conditions for up to five days, including predictions of heavy rainfall in many regions.

mix_items.summary: Researchers in Chile have designed an unlikely new garment for injured penguins—snug red vests threaded with copper and zinc that they hope will help the aquatic birds heal faster.

mix_items.title: Underwater meadows sustain millions in extreme poverty
mix_items.summary: A study provides the first large-scale empirical evidence that seagrass meadows act as a critical safety net for millions of coastal people living in extreme poverty across the Indo-Pacific.

mix_items.title: The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
mix_items.summary: Star formation across the universe has fallen dramatically over the past 4.5 billion years, but astronomers have uncovered a surprising twist: the supply of neutral hydrogen, a key ingredient for making stars, has barely declined. Using China’s FAST radio telescope and data from roughly 2.5 million galaxies observed by DESI, researchers found that star formation was about 2.5 times higher 4.5 billion years ago, while neutral hydrogen levels were only about 1.4 times higher.

mix_items.title: September brings a dazzling Venus and a glowing Harvest Moon
mix_items.summary: September’s sky features brilliant Venus, the Milky Way’s hazy center, and the seasonal turning point of the equinox. The month ends with a glowing Harvest Moon rising near Saturn and faint Neptune.

mix_items.title: Women bear the brunt of alcohol-related fear, Australian research finds
mix_items.summary: Women are nearly three-quarters more likely than men to experience fear because of other people's alcohol consumption, University of Queensland research published in the International Journal of Drug Policy has found.

mix_items.title: When we eat helps set the liver's metabolic rhythms
mix_items.summary: When we think about metabolism, we usually ask, "What did I eat? How much sugar, fat or protein was in the meal?" But through our research, we have become interested in another question: "When did I eat it?" This matters because metabolism does not work at the same pace throughout the day.

mix_items.title: Residential context has larger impact on ovarian cancer survival in Black women
mix_items.summary: Residential context has a stronger association with survival for Black than White women with epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC), according to a study published online Aug. 10 in JAMA Network Open.

mix_items.title: Targeting two proteins to prevent pulmonary hypertension
mix_items.summary: UIC researchers have identified two therapeutic targets for pulmonary arterial hypertension, an as-yet-incurable disease that can be caused by a parasite laying eggs in the abdomen. The targets represent an opportunity to diagnose, prevent and treat the life-threatening condition. The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: Exercise alters brain activity during cognitive tasks, advanced imaging finds
mix_items.summary: Researchers at AIST, in collaboration with the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center in the United States, examined changes in brain activity during cognitive tasks before and after acute aerobic exercise in healthy young and older adults. The study is published in the Journal of Magnetic Resonance Imaging.

mix_items.title: How HIV affects the eyes of aging adults
mix_items.summary: Older adults with well-controlled HIV may have a higher prevalence of certain eye conditions, particularly dry eye, compared with similar adults without HIV, according to a new study led by a University of Colorado Anschutz Department of Ophthalmology faculty member.

mix_items.title: Daraxonrasib demonstrates initial antitumor activity in RAS-mutant lung cancer
mix_items.summary: Daraxonrasib, an oral RAS inhibitor therapy, achieved durable responses in pretreated patients with RAS-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in a phase 1/2 trial led by The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

mix_items.title: Less-intensive drug combination is more effective in treating acute myeloid leukemia, clinical trial finds
mix_items.summary: Investigators from the Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute have found that adults with newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) receiving a less-intensive combination of azacitidine and venetoclax had more than twice as much time before treatment failed, the leukemia returned or worsened, or they died, compared with patients receiving intensive chemotherapy. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the findings could change the initial treatment approach for many patients with AML.

mix_items.title: Autism diagnoses rising fastest among girls and women, study finds
mix_items.summary: A new Saint Louis University study of nearly a decade of health records finds that the recent rise in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnoses is being driven largely by girls and women, who are being identified at significantly higher rates than in years past, often years later than boys and men.

mix_items.title: Genetic pathway offers new insight into timing of early brain development
mix_items.summary: Melbourne researchers have uncovered a critical signaling pathway that controls the timing of brain development, shedding new light on how neurodevelopmental disorders may develop. The research, led by Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI) and published in Nature Communications, has revealed the genetic processes that shape brain development and what can happen when they are disrupted.

mix_items.title: In Canada, immigration status is associated with length of ICU stay after stroke
mix_items.summary: Among people who have a stroke in Canada, immigrants were admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) at similar rates to long-term residents or people who were born in Canada, but they were more likely to have longer stays in the ICU, according to a study published Sept. 2, 2026, in Neurology.

mix_items.title: Mini-tumors reveal new drug combinations for liver cancer
mix_items.summary: Liver cancer is difficult to treat because tumors vary greatly from patient to patient. Researchers at the University of Basel have captured this diversity by creating a collection of mini-tumors, which they use to systematically search for new treatment options. They tested more than 1,600 compounds using these organoids and used the results to develop promising drug combinations.

mix_items.title: Novel spatial technology may improve our understanding of cancer biology
mix_items.summary: Northwestern Medicine scientists have developed a novel high-resolution spatial genomics platform that may enhance future research into how genome organization and genetic alterations contribute to disease development, including cancer, as detailed in a recent study published in Nature Methods.

mix_items.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

mix_items.title: Researchers followed 400,000 kids for 20 years and found a lasting pre-K advantage
mix_items.summary: A 20-year study of 400,000 students found that children who attended public school pre-K earned better grades and test scores through high school than those in other childcare settings. Better-trained teachers and earlier exposure to structured classrooms may help explain why the advantage lasted so long.

mix_items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based meat alternatives. Every one contained fungal toxins
mix_items.summary: Every one of 212 plant-based meat alternatives and drinks tested in the UK contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, though concentrations remained below recommended EU guideline levels. Researchers say the bigger question is whether regularly eating large amounts of these foods could lead to potentially concerning cumulative exposure over time.

mix_items.title: The ex-oil executive trying to wean us off fossil fuels
mix_items.summary: Samantha Cooper once helped power the oil industry. Now she’s fighting to end its hold on our future The post The ex-oil executive trying to wean us off fossil fuels appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: A major Alzheimer’s risk gene may shrink brain cells years before symptoms
mix_items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a possible reason why the Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 can disrupt the brain long before memory problems begin. In mice, APOE4 increased a protein called Nell2, shrinking neurons and making memory circuits unusually active. That early hyperactivity predicted worse memory later in life. Reducing Nell2 in adult mice reversed the abnormal changes, raising hopes for a new way to intervene before Alzheimer’s progresses.

mix_items.title: The dental crown of the future could be 3D-printed while you wait
mix_items.summary: Researchers have found a way to slash the processing time for 3D-printed zirconia crowns from as much as 100 hours to under 30 minutes. The advance could eventually let dentists print strong, customized permanent crowns for patients within a single appointment.

mix_items.title: A hidden “on switch” in human DNA has finally been decoded
mix_items.summary: Researchers have used AI to uncover the DNA signature of a key genetic “switch” involved in turning genes on. After analyzing about 500,000 DNA sequences, the model identified the initiator in roughly 60% of human genes. The breakthrough could help predict the effects of harmful mutations and eventually contribute to decoding the broader genetic instructions that control gene activity throughout the body.

mix_items.title: Experimental compound helps burn fat without muscle loss
mix_items.summary: A decades-old compound may point to a new way of treating obesity by making the body burn more energy rather than simply reducing appetite. In mice, TOFA increased energy use by as much as 18%, reduced body fat without significant muscle loss, and improved blood sugar, triglycerides, and fatty liver disease. It also produced stronger results when combined with GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound.

mix_items.title: Cannabis use linked to 37% higher stroke risk in massive study
mix_items.summary: A massive analysis involving more than 100 million people has found strong links between recreational drug use and stroke, including among younger adults. Cocaine was associated with nearly double the risk of stroke, amphetamines with more than double the risk, and cannabis with a 37% increase.

mix_items.title: This common vitamin was linked to 13% better cognitive scores
mix_items.summary: Older adults with mild cognitive impairment and sleep problems who took at least 5,000 IU of vitamin D daily scored more than 13% higher on a cognitive test than those taking none. The preliminary findings suggest vitamin D could be worth studying as a potentially modifiable factor during an early window of cognitive decline.

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.
